title: A fence around the Opus worker
eyebrow: You told me the Opus worker is the lead's alone; this turns that from a written request into a refusal the machine enforces

content.label: What changes
content.lead: One rule, checked every time anything asks for the Opus worker.

rows: goes through, exactly as it does today
An ordinary session in this repo
refused, and told to start the work with the lead instead
Anything asking for a different helper
untouched — searching, researching and rendering all carry on

blocks.text: The refusal says what to do instead rather than only saying no, so a session that reaches for the worker out of habit is pointed at the lead rather than left guessing.

This is in. Ten cases were run against it by hand before it landed: the worker is refused to an ordinary session and to every other helper, let through to the lead, and nothing else is affected in any of them. It now runs before every request for a helper, alongside the four checks that were already there.

Then it was run for real, in two fresh sessions rather than on paper. One asked for the worker straight out and was turned down, quoting the refusal back word for word. The other started the lead, and the lead's own request for the worker went through and came back answered. Both halves hold: the thing you caught is stopped, and the thing that must keep working still works.

content.label: Why it can be enforced at all
content.lead: A rule is only worth writing if the machine can tell who is asking. It can, and that was checked in a throwaway project before any of this was built.

blocks.text: What you saw was reproduced first, from an ordinary session, before anything was touched: it asked for the Opus worker outright, nothing stopped it, and the worker answered in about two seconds. Four checks already run before any tool is used here and none of them looks at this.

rows: When one helper calls another, do our own checks learn who called
When an ordinary session calls, is anything named
no — the name is simply absent, which is what makes the two cases tellable apart

content.label: What it does not do
content.lead: The fence is one rule and nothing more.

blocks.text: It does not change what the lead or the worker are told to do, it does not fence any other helper, and it does not stop you calling anything yourself. It is also not a lock: it holds inside this repo, where our own checks run.

The rule is now written down in one place, in the project's own rulebook, next to the other standing rules — one line saying it and one pointing at the check, rather than a description of how the check works.

You wrote it in the plural — the worker is for Fable agents to call. The lead is the only one there is, so it is named on its own. If a second one ever exists it has to be named too, deliberately: the alternative is a list of who else may call, and that list is the thing that grows quietly until the rule means nothing.

decisions.title: A refusal, not a written request
decisions.why: Your call. A line of text asking sessions to behave would have let the same thing you caught happen again, and you would only have found out by spotting it a second time.

decisions.title: The lead is the only way through, with no list of exceptions
decisions.why: You said the worker is the lead's alone. A list of who else may call is the thing that quietly grows until the rule means nothing, so there is no list — one name, and everything else is refused.

decisions.title: The rule is exercised by being made to fail
decisions.why: A check that only ever passes proves nothing. This one is tested from both ends — an ordinary session refused, the lead let through, everything else left alone — and then it was broken on purpose, twice, to watch it go red each way before being put back.

next.if_nothing: Nothing — this is done and in. The worker is the lead's alone from now on.

steps.step: Run one real job through the lead and see whether its briefs hold up
